A 68-year-old woman presented with a 10-day history of hemoptysis and a 1-month history of mild cough, sputum production, and rhinorrhea. Her past medical history was unremarkable, with no malignancy, immunosuppressive therapy, diabetes mellitus, or vasculitis. On examination, vital signs were normal. Mild wheezing was auscultated bilaterally; neurologic and skin findings were normal. Laboratory tests showed an elevated C-reactive protein level of 7 mg/dL (reference: 0–0.3 mg/dL) and a normal white-cell count with a neutrophil count of 3.97 × 10^3/μL. HIV testing was negative. Initial microbiologic studies—including bacterial cultures, acid-fast bacillus smear and culture of sputum, blood cultures (bacterial and fungal), and respiratory viral serologies—were all negative. 

A chest radiograph demonstrated multiple nodules and masses of various sizes in both lung fields, some with cavitation. Chest CT (lung window) showed cavitary and noncavitary nodules and masses with faint surrounding ground-glass opacity (“halo sign”). Cavitary lesions had thick, irregular walls with septa-like structures; on mediastinal windows, one lesion contained a hypoattenuating area. A coronal maximum intensity projection image showed patent vessels within the lesions. A small bilateral pleural effusion was present. 

Antineutrophil cytoplasmic antibody titers (both c-ANCA and p-ANCA) were within normal limits. Bronchoscopy with bronchoalveolar lavage and transbronchial biopsy revealed diffuse granulomatous inflammation but no organisms. Video-assisted thoracoscopic wedge resection of a cavitary lesion was performed. Histopathologic analysis showed diffuse necrotizing granulomatous inflammation and fungal elements. Methenamine silver staining revealed yeast-like structures associated with septate hyphae demonstrating acute-angle branching.

A man in his 50s with a 10-year history of Crohn disease had intermittent bowel obstructions leading to total proctocolectomy and ileostomy. Five weeks after his surgery, he developed a painful, erosive lesion around his stoma on the anterior abdominal wall. No additional cutaneous or mucosal lesions were present.

Painful, erosive lesion present around the stoma on the anterior abdominal wall

A 39-year-old man with a history of treated tuberculosis presented with two weeks of fever, generalized weakness, vague abdominal pain, vomiting, headache, body aches, and moderate nasal bleeding. On examination, he had a 2×1 cm submandibular lymph node and hepatomegaly (7 cm below the costal margin), without gastrointestinal symptoms or skin lesions. Laboratory studies showed urea 18.8 mmol/L, creatinine 141 µmol/L, lipase 182 U/L, myoglobin 108 ng/mL, ferritin >40 000 µg/L, vitamin B12 <111 pmol/L, normal fibrinogen, and triglycerides. Viral serologies were negative. Complete blood count revealed pancytopenia: hemoglobin 6.4 g/dL, WBC 1.7×10^3/µL, ANC 0.9×10^3/µL, platelets 2×10^3/µL. Head CT showed bilateral subdural hemorrhages without midline shift. Whole-body CT demonstrated bilateral pleural effusion, extensive pulmonary consolidation, thrombosis of the celiac artery with splenic infarction, mild hepatomegaly, and massive splenomegaly with infarction. 

Initial peripheral smear showed very few atypical cells; a repeat smear revealed marked leukopenia and 13% abnormal blastoid cells of medium size with fine nuclear chromatin, unevenly distributed coarse basophilic granules, and occasional bilobed nuclei. Bone marrow aspirate was hypercellular with 26% immature metachromatic blasts—cells with eccentric nuclei, abundant cytoplasm, and coarse giant granules—as well as some agranular high N/C blasts and spindle-shaped cells. There was trilineage dysplasia with megaloblastic changes in granulocytes and erythroid precursors, dysplastic megakaryocytes, and frequent mitoses. Both histiocytes and the atypical cells demonstrated erythrophagocytosis.

A 56-year-old nulliparous woman presented 14 months after a supracervical laparoscopic hysterectomy and bilateral salpingo-oophorectomy for menorrhagia, pelvic pain, and large uterine leiomyomas. Her preoperative evaluation included a normal Pap smear; no chest radiograph or endometrial biopsy was obtained. At surgery, an 18–20-week–size uterus (1518 g) was removed via prolonged mechanical morcellation without a containment bag; superficial pelvic endometriosis was noted and cauterized. Final pathology on six uterine fragments demonstrated weakly proliferative endometrium without atypia, adenomyosis, and leiomyoma; the ovaries showed benign parenchyma and endosalpingiosis. 

On presentation, she reported left lower quadrant pain, persistent cough, and shortness of breath. Examination revealed a firm left lower quadrant abdominal mass and a fleshy lesion at the vaginal apex; the cervix was not visualized. PET–CT showed multiple hypermetabolic masses in the pelvis, abdomen, and chest. A core-needle biopsy of a 9 cm left pelvic mass revealed poorly differentiated epithelioid cells with hyperchromatic nuclei in necrosis. Immunohistochemical stains were positive for cytokeratin, vimentin, and CD138, and negative for SMA, EMA, ER, TLE1, HMB45, desmin, myogenin, CD117, BCL2, inhibin, MDN2, CD4, CA125, WT-1, CD45, calretinin, DOG-1, p16, CEA, CK20, HPV, and CD99. A vaginal biopsy showed grade 3 endometrioid adenocarcinoma. Pathology re-review of the hysterectomy and oophorectomy specimens showed no evidence of malignancy.

A woman in her 80s presented with an 8-month history of a growing, painful tumor on her right buttock. The patient felt well otherwise and denied experiencing fevers, chills, sweats, weight loss, or malaise. Her medical history was notable for chronic kidney disease and genital herpes simplex virus (HSV). She reported no history of genital warts, HIV, or inflammatory bowel disease.

Physical examination findings revealed a 5 × 7-cm verrucous, exophytic tumor with scant yellow drainage on the right medial buttock extending to the perianal skin. Findings from the remaining skin examination were normal.

- Bacterial Cultures: Superficial bacterial cultures were obtained from the lesion and grew methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus. Microbial cultures were negative for deep fungal infection and acid-fast bacteria but positive for HSV type 2.- Biopsy and Histology:  Image Title: Clinical and Histological Images (Figure 1)  Image Description: A) Clinical image of verrucous tumor on right medial buttock  B) Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing hyperplastic epidermis with ulceration, necrosis, and dense inflammatory infiltrate  C) Hematoxylin-eosin stain showing plasma cells and focal multinucleated keratinocytes with gray-blue cytoplasm- Immunohistochemistry:  Image Title: Immunohistochemical Staining (Figure 2)  Image Description: Positive staining for herpes simplex virus types 1 and 2 within epithelial cells, including multinucleated keratinocytes
